heading: Stack finds rectangle boundaries
body:
A **monotonic increasing stack** tracks bar indices. When you hit a shorter bar, pop the stack — the current index is the **right boundary**, the index below the popped element is the **left boundary**.

- Width = `right - left - 1`
- Height = popped bar's height
- Avoids O(n²) scanning!

heading: Don't increment after popping
body:
After you pop, the current bar might **also** be shorter than the new stack top. Keep `i` fixed and keep popping until you can push `i`.

This lets one bar serve as the right boundary for multiple taller bars.

label: Crux · Python
code:
stack = []
max_area = 0
i = 0

while i < len(heights):
    if not stack or heights[i] >= heights[stack[-1]]:
        stack.append(i)
        i += 1
    else:
        top = stack.pop()
        right = i - 1
        left = stack[-1] if stack else -1
        area = heights[top] * (right - left)
        max_area = max(max_area, area)

# Empty remaining stack
while stack:
    top = stack.pop()
    width = i - stack[-1] - 1 if stack else i
    area = heights[top] * width
    max_area = max(max_area, area)

q: After popping index `top` from the stack when heights[i] < heights[stack[-1]], how is the width of the rectangle calculated?
explain: The right boundary is i - 1 (the last bar >= heights[top]), and the left boundary is stack[-1] (or -1 if empty). Width = right - left.
